elements.element: Customer owns all deliverables and work product created for it.
elements.evidence: Customer owns Type I Materials, but Type II Materials may also be “created during the Service performance period” and remain owned by IBM or third parties. The clause therefore does not give Customer ownership of all deliverables and work product created for it.

elements.element: Vendor assigns to Customer all right, title, and interest in those deliverables and work product.
elements.evidence: The clause says Customer “will have all right, title, and interest” in Type I Materials, but contains no operative assignment by IBM and does not cover service-created Type II Materials.

elements.element: Vendor retains its pre-existing intellectual property.
elements.evidence: Type II Materials expressly include materials that “preexist the Service” and in which IBM or third parties have all right, title, and interest.

elements.element: Customer receives a licence to any Vendor intellectual property embedded in the deliverables.
elements.evidence: IBM grants a licence to Type II Materials, but the clause does not state that all IBM intellectual property embedded in Customer-owned deliverables is Type II Material or otherwise covered by the licence.

elements.element: The licence to embedded Vendor intellectual property is perpetual.
elements.evidence: The Type II Materials licence is expressly “perpetual.”

elements.element: The licence to embedded Vendor intellectual property is irrevocable.
elements.evidence: The Type II Materials licence is expressly “irrevocable.”

elements.element: The licence to embedded Vendor intellectual property is royalty-free.
elements.evidence: The Type II Materials licence is expressly “royalty-free” and “paid-up.”

elements.element: Customer retains all rights in Customer Data.
elements.evidence: The data language limits certain storage, processing, and use to providing the Services, but it does not state that Customer owns or retains all rights in Customer Data. It also addresses only contact information and personal information processed on Customer’s behalf.

elements.element: There is no joint ownership of deliverables, work product, or Customer Data.
elements.evidence: Type I Materials are allocated entirely to Customer and Type II Materials entirely to IBM or third parties. IBM receives only a licence to Type I Materials, and no joint ownership is created.

elements.element: Vendor owns its generic tools.
elements.evidence: The clause reserves ownership of Type II Materials to IBM or third parties but never identifies or expressly reserves “generic tools,” so the required subject-matter scope is not established.

elements.element: Vendor owns its generic know-how.
elements.evidence: The clause contains no ownership reservation for IBM’s generic know-how, and “Materials” is not stated to include know-how.

elements.element: Customer has a licence or ownership-equivalent right covering all deliverables.
elements.evidence: Customer owns Type I Materials outright and receives a licence to Type II Materials. Together, those provisions provide ownership-equivalent or licensed rights across the two stated categories of Materials.

elements.element: Customer’s rights in the deliverables are perpetual.
elements.evidence: The Type II Materials licence is expressly perpetual, while Customer’s ownership of Type I Materials is not time-limited.

elements.element: Customer’s rights in the deliverables are irrevocable.
elements.evidence: The Type II Materials licence is expressly irrevocable, while Customer’s ownership of Type I Materials is not revocable.

elements.element: Customer’s rights in the deliverables are worldwide.
elements.evidence: The Type II Materials licence is expressly worldwide; Customer’s ownership of Type I Materials is not territorially limited.

elements.element: Customer’s rights in the deliverables are royalty-free.
elements.evidence: The Type II Materials licence is expressly royalty-free and paid-up; no royalty applies to Customer’s owned Type I Materials.

elements.element: Customer may use the deliverables.
elements.evidence: The Type II Materials licence expressly permits Customer to “use” them, and Customer owns Type I Materials.

elements.element: Customer may modify the deliverables.
elements.evidence: The Type II Materials licence expressly permits Customer to “modify” them, and Customer’s ownership of Type I Materials includes the corresponding copyright rights.

elements.element: Customer may sublicense the deliverables.
elements.evidence: The Type II Materials licence expressly permits sublicensing, and Customer may license its owned Type I Materials.

elements.element: Customer may exercise its deliverable rights for its business.
elements.evidence: The Type II Materials rights are expressly granted “for Customer’s business purposes,” and no narrower purpose restriction applies to Customer-owned Type I Materials.

result.reason: The redline adds the principal fallback licence attributes for Type II Materials, but it does not expressly reserve IBM’s generic tools and know-how, so the complete fallback is not met. It also falls materially short of the preferred position: service-created Type II Materials remain Vendor- or third-party-owned, there is no assignment, embedded Vendor IP is not expressly covered, and Customer’s ownership of Customer Data is omitted. The changes do not introduce a direct contradiction, but they are not minimal because they fail to achieve either complete level and the data-use revision does not supply the required Customer Data ownership language.
